story: Fifteen years after Muammar Gaddafi was killed in a drainage pipe, Libya still has two governments, two parliaments and, in practice, two armies, sitting on Africa's largest oil reserves. The internationally recognised government in Tripoli under Abdul Hamid Dbeibah controls the west. The east and south answer to the 82-year-old field marshal Khalifa Haftar and a rival cabinet under Osama Hamad. The 2021 elections that were meant to end this were cancelled days before polling, and both camps have found the division comfortable.

2026 showed the cost. On 8 May, fighting with heavy weapons between Tripoli-aligned security forces and local militias forced Libya's largest refinery, at Zawiya, to shut, with shells landing in civilian neighbourhoods (Security Council Report). Drone strikes later hit refinery facilities, and parts of the country suffered fuel and power shortages despite sitting on all that oil. Then, on 30 August, after months of UN-led talks, the rival sides signed an agreement in Tripoli to hold national elections within two years, which the Security Council called an important step (Africanews). Libyans have heard promises like this before. The question is whether the men who benefit from the split will let a vote remove them.
briefing.power: No single authority. The UN-recognised Government of National Unity and a Presidential Council govern from Tripoli; the eastern House of Representatives backs a rival Government of National Stability and Haftar's Libyan National Army. Armed groups hold real power on the ground in both halves.
briefing.holders: Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah in Tripoli; Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar in the east.
